metadata.summary: This joint consensus addresses pre-operative characterization of ovarian and other adnexal tumors and assessment of disease spread. It evaluates ultrasound, imaging, tumor markers and prediction models, and presents 18 evidence-graded statements alongside pathways for specialist referral and further assessment. Screening, follow-up methods and economic evaluations are outside its stated scope.

target_population: Patients with newly diagnosed adnexal lesions
Patients with symptoms suggestive of an adnexal mass
Patients with an incidental adnexal mass on imaging
Patients undergoing pre-operative evaluation for cytoreductive surgery

therapies_index.name: conservative treatment
approved_indications: Benign adnexal lesions may be managed conservatively, depending on the clinical context.

therapies_index.name: less radical surgical treatment
approved_indications: Benign adnexal lesions may be suitable for a less radical operation, depending on the clinical context.

therapies_index.name: cytoreductive surgery
approved_indications: Patients with ovarian cancer may undergo evaluation for cytoreductive surgery; selection must take the overall clinical context into account.

therapies_index.name: fertility-sparing surgery
approved_indications: Mentioned as a consideration when assessing whether MRI can confirm the diagnosis of the primary lesion.

recommendations.statement: Expert ultrasound examiners (Level III) provide the most accurate subjective distinction between benign and malignant ovarian tumors.
recommendations.rationale: The accuracy of ultrasonography depends on the examiner’s expertise.

recommendations.statement: When an expert ultrasound examiner is unavailable, ultrasound-based diagnostic models can help clinicians distinguish benign from malignant ovarian tumors.
Prefer the IOTA Simple Rules risk model or the IOTA ADNEX model over CA 125, HE4, or ROMA for distinguishing benign from malignant ovarian tumors.
recommendations.rationale: The specified ultrasound-based models perform better for this distinction.

recommendations.statement: Use the IOTA ADNEX model or the IOTA Simple Rules risk model in preference to existing morphological scoring systems, including the RMI.
recommendations.rationale: These models outperform the existing morphological scoring systems.

recommendations.statement: The IOTA ADNEX model can help distinguish benign tumors, borderline tumors, early- or advanced-stage ovarian cancer, and secondary metastatic tumors.
recommendations.rationale: The model provides predictions for multiple tumor categories.

recommendations.statement: Trigger additional investigations to identify the primary organ when the IOTA ADNEX model predicts a risk of a secondary metastatic tumor above 10%.
recommendations.context: Consensus: 5% threshold, 10% (n=2); 10% threshold, 75% (n=15); 15% threshold, 0% (n=0); 20% threshold, 0% (n=0); abstain, 15% (n=3).

recommendations.statement: CA 125 is the strongest available single-protein biomarker for characterizing ovarian tumors before surgery, but it is not useful for ovarian cancer screening.
recommendations.rationale: CA 125 has limited sensitivity and specificity in early disease and relatively low specificity overall.

recommendations.statement: Compared with CA 125 alone, neither HE4 nor ROMA improves discrimination between benign and malignant masses.
Adding CA 125 does not improve the ability of ultrasound-based risk models to distinguish benign from malignant tumors.
In suspected malignancy, CA 125 can help distinguish malignant tumor subtypes, including borderline tumors, early- and advanced-stage primary ovarian cancers, and secondary metastatic tumors.
In selected cases, CEA may help distinguish primary ovarian cancer from secondary ovarian tumors.
CA 19-9 can assist in distinguishing secondary metastatic tumors in the ovary.

MRI incorporating dynamic contrast-enhanced and diffusion-weighted functional sequences is not a first-line investigation, but it may follow ultrasonography to further distinguish benign, malignant, and borderline masses.
recommendations.source_heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)

recommendations.statement: If the initial ultrasound raises suspicion of a secondary metastatic tumor, PET-CT and whole-body diffusion MRI can help identify a non-ovarian primary site as a second step.
recommendations.source_heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)

recommendations.statement: PET-CT cannot reliably distinguish borderline tumors from benign tumors.
recommendations.rationale: Its diagnostic value for this distinction is low.
recommendations.source_heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)

recommendations.statement: Imaging by itself cannot reliably establish the full extent of peritoneal carcinomatosis, particularly low-volume disease, or involvement of the mesenteric and bowel serosa.
recommendations.source_heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)

recommendations.statement: Do not base surgical decisions about the predicted resectability of peritoneal tumor solely on imaging.
recommendations.rationale: Imaging cannot reliably depict the entire extent of disease at key peritoneal sites.
recommendations.source_heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)

recommendations.statement: Do not yet use circulating cell-free DNA or circulating tumor cells routinely to distinguish benign from malignant ovarian masses.
recommendations.rationale: Their diagnostic value remains uncertain, and further validation is needed.
recommendations.source_heading: Statement on circulating cell-free DNA and tumor cells (Statement 18)

artifacts.clinical_relevance: These patterns help an examiner narrow the differential diagnosis and recognize findings that warrant assessment for malignancy or a non-ovarian primary tumor.

artifacts.title: Table 2 Summary of main models and scoring systems for pre-operative diagnosis of ovarian tumors

rows: Simple descriptors: classification as benign or malignant

Benign descriptor (BD) 1: unilocular tumor with ground-glass echogenicity in a premenopausal woman. BD2: unilocular tumor with mixed echogenicity and acoustic shadows in a pre-menopausal woman. BD3: unilocular anechoic tumor with regular walls and maximum diameter of lesion <10 cm. BD4: other unilocular tumor with regular walls. Malignant descriptor (MD) 1: tumor with ascites and at least moderate color Doppler blood flow in a post-menopausal woman. MD2: age >50 years and CA 125 >100 U/mL.
Does not estimate risk; uses clinical, ultrasound and CA 125 information; calculation does not require a computer.
CA 125, menopausal status and an ultrasound score comprising five binary findings: multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites and evidence of metastases on abdominal ultrasound.
Does not estimate risk; uses clinical, ultrasound and CA 125 information; calculation does not require a computer; online calculators are available.
Simple Rules: classification as benign, inconclusive or malignant

10 binary features, comprising five benign and five malignant features. Benign: unilocular cyst; smooth multilocular cyst with largest diameter <100 mm; solid areas with largest diameter <7 mm; acoustic shadows; no color Doppler vascularization. Malignant: irregular solid tumor; irregular multilocular solid tumor with largest diameter ≥100 mm; ascites; ≥4 papillary projections; very strong color Doppler vascularization.
Does not estimate risk; assigns one of three groups from dichotomized ultrasound findings; usable without a computer; smartphone app available.
LR2: risk model based on logistic regression
Age (years), acoustic shadows, ascites, papillary projections with blood flow, maximum diameter of the largest solid component and irregular internal cyst walls.
Estimates risk using clinical and ultrasound information; requires a computer; smartphone app available.
Simple Rules risk: risk model based on logistic regression
The 10 binary features of Simple Rules and type of center (oncology center vs other).

Estimates risk from dichotomized ultrasound features, extending Simple Rules to provide risk estimates; online calculator and incorporation into ultrasound machines from some manufacturers are available.
ADNEX without CA 125: risk model based on multinomial logistic regression

Age (years), maximum lesion diameter (mm), maximum diameter of the largest solid component (mm), number of papillary projections (ordinal), acoustic shadows, ascites, more than 10 cyst locules and type of center (oncology center vs other).

Estimates risk, including risk for four malignant subtypes; uses clinical and ultrasound information while avoiding subjective predictors a priori, such as color score or irregular cyst walls; requires a computer; smartphone app, online calculator and incorporation into ultrasound machines from some manufacturers are available.
ADNEX with CA 125: risk model based on multinomial logistic regression
Variables used for ADNEX without CA 125, plus serum CA 125 (IU/L).

Estimates risk, including risk for four malignant subtypes; uses clinical, ultrasound and CA 125 information while avoiding subjective predictors a priori, such as color score or irregular cyst walls; requires a computer; smartphone app, online calculator and incorporation into ultrasound machines from some manufacturers are available.

artifacts.description: The malignant descriptor MD2 belongs to the Simple descriptors criteria. The table distinguishes classification tools that do not give an individual risk estimate from regression models that do.
artifacts.summary: The table compares the inputs and practical characteristics of Simple descriptors, RMI, Simple Rules, LR2, Simple Rules risk and the two ADNEX variants. It identifies which tools estimate malignancy risk and which can also estimate risks for malignant subtypes.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Selecting an appropriate model depends on its required inputs, the available expertise and whether the decision requires a category, an individual risk estimate or differentiation among malignant subtypes.

artifacts.title: Figure 2 Flowchart of steps recommended to distinguish between benign and malignant tumors and to direct patients towards appropriate treatment pathway
artifacts.description: Step 1: For symptoms suggesting an adnexal mass, or an incidental adnexal mass on imaging, begin with ultrasonography; examination of a suspected ovarian mass should be performed by an expert sonographer. Step 2: If the examination identifies normal ovaries or physiological changes, the lesion falls within O-RADS 1; otherwise, the IOTA ADNEX model could be used to estimate malignancy risk. Step 3: Use the resulting O-RADS categories 2–5 to guide management and the selection of patients for referral to a dedicated gynecological oncology center. A suspicious malignant mass warrants referral to that center; a suspected non-gynecological primary tumor calls for referral to the relevant specialist, while a benign lesion may be followed conservatively or considered for less radical surgery according to clinical context. Decisions also account for symptoms, preferences, history, tumor markers and clinical and radiological findings rather than one diagnostic modality alone.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart sets out initial ultrasound-based assessment and risk stratification of an adnexal mass, followed by management or specialist referral. The accompanying consensus describes how IOTA ADNEX and O-RADS categories can inform that route.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports appropriate triage while avoiding a management decision based solely on one test.

artifacts.title: Figure 3 Flowchart of steps necessary to differentiate between subgroups of malignancy and extent of disease within gynecological oncology centers
artifacts.description: Step 1: Within a gynecological oncology center, assess the lesion by expert ultrasound or apply the IOTA ADNEX model alongside a tumor-marker profile comprising CA 125 and CEA, with other markers in specific cases; this combination can often suggest a malignant subtype. Step 2: If available, diffusion- and perfusion-weighted MRI can help confirm the diagnosis of the primary lesion, particularly when fertility-sparing surgery is being considered. Step 3: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy, obtain CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to exclude secondary cancers, thromboembolic events and multifocal intraparenchymal distant metastases that would preclude resectability. Step 4: An expert multidisciplinary team determines individualized management using the diagnostic findings, symptoms, preferences and previous surgical, medical and reproductive history. The figure notes that ‘early stage’ and ‘advanced stage’ may differ between ADNEX model groupings (stage I vs stages III–IV) and oncological groupings (stages I–II vs stages I–IV).
artifacts.summary: The flowchart addresses malignant subtype assessment, evaluation of disease extent and planning within a gynecological oncology center. It combines expert assessment, selected markers, possible MRI, mandatory pre-operative CT and multidisciplinary decision-making.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps characterize suspected malignancy and identify findings relevant to operative planning without treating imaging alone as a sufficient basis for predicting resectability.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: ESGO, ISUOG, IOTA and ESGE jointly developed evidence-based statements about imaging, biomarkers and prediction models for diagnosing ovarian tumors before surgery and assessing carcinomatosis. Their international multidisciplinary group included 19 clinical and research experts and a patient representative. After critical appraisal of the literature, the group discussed draft statements, voted twice and revised or removed statements according to consensus. Agreement was reached on 18 statements. This document presents those statements and their supporting evidence.

document_sections.heading: RESPONSIBILITIES
document_sections.content: The statements express the authors’ consensus on approaches to pre-operative diagnosis and assessment of disease spread, based on available evidence. Clinicians remain responsible for applying independent judgment to each patient’s circumstances; the authors provide no warranty and disclaim responsibility for use of the statements.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Accurate characterization of a newly detected adnexal lesion is essential for choosing an appropriate care pathway. A mass suspicious for malignancy warrants referral to a gynecological oncology center for specialist care, in line with ESGO definitions and other guidelines. A suspected non-gynecological primary tumor calls for referral to the relevant specialist. A benign lesion may instead be monitored, managed conservatively or treated with less radical surgery, according to clinical circumstances. Decisions should integrate symptoms, preferences, medical and surgical history, tumor markers, and clinical and imaging findings; no single diagnostic method should determine care on its own. The consensus addresses diagnosis before surgery and assessment of disease spread, but not screening, follow-up methods or economic evaluation of the diagnostic approaches discussed.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: An eight-step consensus process was chaired by Christina Fotopoulou and Dirk Timmerman; Figure 1 depicts the process. ESGO, ISUOG, IOTA and ESGE nominated 19 experts: eight members of ESGO, five of ISUOG, four of IOTA and two of ESGE. Their clinical expertise comprised seven gynecologists with an ultrasound focus, two radiologists and 10 gynecological oncologists. They contributed personal expertise rather than representing the nominating societies. A patient representative who chaired an ENGAGe clinical-trial project also participated. An initial group call established the purpose and scope. A MEDLINE search examined relevant English-language studies published between 1 May 2015 and 1 May 2020. High-quality systematic reviews, meta-analyses and validation cohorts received priority, although lower-level evidence was considered; editorials, letters and case reports were excluded. Reference lists were checked, and full articles were distributed to the group. FP supplied methodological and medical-writing support without voting. The chairs drafted statements for group discussion. At the next call, all 20 participants took part in binary voting on each proposal, with abstention permitted for insufficient expertise or a potentially influential conflict of interest. Proposals lacking consensus were removed. Voters could suggest changes; the chairs revised statements where needed, and the group voted again under the same rules. Consensus was achieved on 18 statements, presented with evidence levels and grades.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS General remarks
document_sections.content: Excluding borderline ovarian tumors and non-gynecological primary tumors, including gastrointestinal or breast primaries, appears to improve the measured performance of biochemical and imaging tests. The literature assessment nevertheless included studies of all adnexal tumor types to better reflect clinical practice.

document_sections.heading: Ultrasonography
document_sections.content: Transvaginal ultrasound is commonly treated as first-line imaging for adnexal pathology. Accuracy in distinguishing benign from malignant masses depends on operator expertise. European gynecological ultrasound training requirements define three expertise levels. Level III denotes an expert likely to devote most professional time to gynecological scanning or related teaching, research and development. Level II requires at least 2000 gynecological scans during training and at least 500 examinations each year to retain competence. Level I requires at least 300 supervised examinations under a Level II practitioner or an experienced Level I practitioner with at least 2 years’ regular practice, followed by at least 300 examinations each year. In a prospective randomized controlled trial, women assessed by a Level III examiner underwent significantly fewer unnecessary major procedures and had shorter inpatient stays than women assessed by a Level II sonographer. Expert subjective ultrasound assessment performs exceptionally well in separating benign from malignant ovarian tumors and can often suggest a particular histological subtype. Table 1 summarizes characteristic clinical and ultrasound features of adnexal tumor subtypes.

document_sections.heading: Risk of malignancy index (RMI) and risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA)
document_sections.content: RMI combines menopausal status, a transvaginal ultrasound score and serum CA 125. Studies have evaluated its ability to classify adnexal masses. RMI-II, RMI-III and RMI-IV have shown no significant diagnostic advantage over RMI-I. ROMA combines CA 125 and HE4. In pooled data used to inform referral, Westwood et al found ROMA and RMI-I performed similarly after excluding borderline tumors and non-epithelial cancers. A later meta-analysis found RMI-I more specific than ROMA in pre-menopausal women, but similar performance for detecting ovarian cancer in postmenopausal women with an adnexal mass. RMI does not provide an estimated malignancy probability and depends heavily on CA 125; consequently, its sensitivity is relatively low for early invasive and borderline disease, particularly before menopause.

document_sections.heading: IOTA methods
document_sections.content: IOTA published standardized terminology for describing adnexal lesions in 2000 and subsequently developed logistic-regression prediction models. In external validation, Van Holsbeke et al found LR1, which has 12 variables, and LR2, which has six variables, outperformed 12 other models, including RMI; LR2 was simpler to apply. Sayasneh et al found less-experienced sonographers could classify benign and malignant masses accurately with LR1. IOTA Simple Rules use five benign and five malignant ultrasound features. They classify about 80% of masses, leaving the remainder inconclusive. The Simple Rules risk model estimates an individual malignancy risk from those ultrasound features. Four benign and two malignant Simple Descriptors permit an immediate pattern-based classification in about 43% of masses. A sequential strategy of Simple Descriptors, Simple Rules and expert subjective assessment achieved high accuracy. One systematic review and meta-analysis found Simple Rules and LR2 performed better than other scoring systems, including RMI. Another meta-analysis also supported those findings and reported that Simple Rules followed by expert assessment of inconclusive masses matched expert ultrasound performance. Simple Rules have entered national guidelines and were considered the principal strategy in an international consensus report. In a randomized controlled trial comparing an RCOG protocol based on RMI with IOTA Simple Rules triage, the IOTA approach reduced surgical intervention without increasing delayed cancer diagnoses. Adding CA 125 and HE4 to Simple Rules, whether or not an expert also assessed the mass, offered no additional characterization benefit and cost more than the sequential three-step strategy. IOTA ADNEX estimates benign versus malignant status and distinguishes borderline tumors, Stage I primary cancers, Stage II–IV primary cancers and secondary metastatic tumors. It was developed and validated using measurements by experienced examiners. External validations found good-to-excellent subtype discrimination and greater clinical value than RMI; a further study supported its use by Level II examiners. In a multicenter cohort comprising 4905 masses at 17 centers, comparison of six model configurations identified IOTA ADNEX and the IOTA Simple Rules risk model as the best for characterizing presenting adnexal lesions. Table 2 compares the inputs, outputs and practical features of the principal diagnostic models and scoring systems.

document_sections.heading: Gynecologic Imaging Reporting and Data System (GI-RADS)
document_sections.content: Amor et al introduced GI-RADS in 2009 and prospectively validated it in a multicenter study 2 years later. Its five categories assign estimated probabilities of malignancy: GI-RADS 1, definitively benign, 0%; GI-RADS 2, very probably benign, <1%; GI-RADS 3, probably benign, 1–4%; GI-RADS 4, probably malignant, 5–20%; and GI-RADS 5, very probably malignant, >20%. Subsequent studies found it useful for assessing malignant adnexal masses in surgical candidates. Combining GI-RADS with CA 125 identifies high-risk masses better than CA 125 alone.

document_sections.heading: Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS)
document_sections.content: The ultrasound O-RADS lexicon, published in 2018, standardizes descriptions of normal ovaries and adnexal lesions. An associated triage system assigns risk categories using either O-RADS descriptors or malignancy risk calculated with IOTA ADNEX. At the time of the consensus, neither the descriptors nor the triage system had undergone external validation. Basha et al retrospectively applied O-RADS to 647 masses collected before its development. They found significantly greater sensitivity than GI-RADS and IOTA Simple Rules, slightly lower specificity that was not statistically significant, and similar reliability.

document_sections.heading: Statements on ultrasonography (Statements 1–6)
document_sections.content: Statement 1: Expert Level III subjective ultrasound assessment has the strongest performance for distinguishing benign from malignant ovarian tumors. Level of evidence: 1a; Grade of statement: A; consensus yes, 95% (n=19), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 2: When an expert examiner is unavailable, ultrasound diagnostic models can help clinicians make that distinction. Level of evidence: 2a; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 90% (n=18), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 10% (n=2). Statement 3: IOTA Simple Rules risk model or IOTA ADNEX model is preferable to CA 125, HE4 or ROMA for this distinction because the ultrasound models perform better. Level of evidence: 2b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 95% (n=19), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 4: IOTA ADNEX model and IOTA Simple Rules risk model are recommended over existing morphological scores, including RMI, because they outperform them. Level of evidence: 1b; Grade of statement: A; consensus yes, 95% (n=19), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 5: The multiclass IOTA ADNEX model helps distinguish benign and borderline tumors, early- and advanced-stage ovarian cancers, and secondary metastases. Level of evidence: 3b; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 85% (n=17), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 15% (n=3). Statement 6: Additional investigations for a primary tumor elsewhere should be triggered when IOTA ADNEX predicts a secondary metastatic tumor risk above 10%. Level of evidence: 5; Grade of statement: D; votes for a 5% threshold, 10% (n=2); a 10% threshold, 75% (n=15); a 15% threshold, 0% (n=0); a 20% threshold, 0% (n=0); abstain, 15% (n=3).

document_sections.heading: Tumor markers
document_sections.content: A systematic quantitative review identified CA 125 as the best available single-protein marker for diagnosing benign, borderline and malignant ovarian tumors. Its sensitivity and specificity are inadequate in early disease, and its overall specificity is relatively low, although it can inform treatment choices for suspicious masses. Pooled analyses suggest body mass index and ethnicity may affect CA 125 concentrations; age, pregnancy, inflammation, fibroids and endometriosis also influence them. Studies and meta-analyses have examined HE4 as a possible complement, particularly for distinguishing benign endometriotic and inflammatory lesions in younger women. Adding markers as in ROMA has not significantly improved benign–malignant discrimination over CA 125 alone. A broader profile adding CEA and/or CA 19-9 is mainly useful for distinguishing gastrointestinal or pancreatic metastases from primary ovarian malignancy. Figure 2 presents the recommended flowchart for distinguishing benign and malignant tumors and directing care.

document_sections.heading: Statements on tumor markers (Statements 7–12)
document_sections.content: Statement 7: CA 125 is the best single-protein biomarker for pre-operative tumor characterization, but is not useful for ovarian cancer screening. Level of evidence: 2b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 95% (n=19), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 8: Neither HE4 nor ROMA improves benign–malignant discrimination over CA 125 alone. Level of evidence: 2b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 70% (n=14), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 30% (n=6). Statement 9: Adding CA 125 does not improve ultrasound risk models’ discrimination of benign and malignant tumors. Level of evidence: 2b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 60% (n=12), no, 10% (n=2), abstain, 30% (n=6). Statement 10: In suspected malignancy, CA 125 helps distinguish borderline, early- and advanced-stage primary cancers and secondary metastatic tumors. Level of evidence: 2b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 90% (n=18), no, 5% (n=1), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 11: In selected cases, CEA may help distinguish primary ovarian cancer from secondary ovarian tumors. Level of evidence: 3b; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 90% (n=18), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 10% (n=2). Statement 12: CA 19-9 can assist in identifying secondary metastatic ovarian tumors. Level of evidence: 3b; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 75% (n=15), no, 5% (n=1), abstain, 20% (n=4).

document_sections.heading: Magnetic resonance imaging
document_sections.content: Reports indicate that MRI, alone or with CT, can accurately predict peritoneal carcinomatosis before cytoreductive surgery, particularly when interpreted by an experienced radiologist. A prospective study found IOTA LR2 more specific than an experienced radiologist’s subjective MRI interpretation for benign–malignant discrimination, with similar sensitivity. Pooled studies found that adding diffusion-weighted imaging improved discrimination between benign tumors and ovarian cancer, especially in Caucasian populations; some data also suggest usefulness for predicting resectability. The size of that benefit still requires validation in large multicenter prospective randomized studies. Combining dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging and anatomical sequences under the 5-point O-RADS MRI score shows promise when ultrasound leaves a mass indeterminate. Adding volume quantification may help distinguish type I from type II epithelial ovarian cancers. Evidence about effects of these newer techniques on clinical decisions remains limited, and larger studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: Computed tomography
document_sections.content: Dedicated multidetector CT with standardized peritoneal carcinomatosis index forms is commonly used to assess tumor spread and carcinomatosis. In an expert setting, a pre-operative radiological peritoneal carcinomatosis index performed poorly as a triage test for complete cytoreduction without macroscopic residual disease. A retrospective analysis found pre-operative CT highly specific but relatively insensitive for involvement of key surgical sites. Studies predicting unresectability or incomplete cytoreduction reported substantial losses of accuracy when their CT findings were tested in other cohorts. CT therefore should not, on its own, determine peritoneal resectability or exclude surgery; the full clinical context matters. Its availability makes it useful initially to identify findings that may preclude cytoreductive surgery, including large or multifocal intraparenchymal distant metastases, acute thromboembolic events and prognosis-limiting secondary metastatic tumors. Preliminary radiomics results are promising, but larger validation studies are needed before routine use.

document_sections.heading: Positron emission tomography-computed tomography
document_sections.content: PET-CT may help distinguish malignant ovarian tumors from borderline or benign lesions, although lower fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in clear cell and mucinous invasive subtypes can reduce its performance. It may also help identify lymph-node metastases, particularly beyond the abdomen, or clarify lesions at sites where the result would alter care, such as the chest. PET-CT does not appear useful for defining the full extent of ovarian peritoneal spread, particularly on bowel and mesenteric serosa, and does not predict resectability reliably at those sites, especially with low-volume disease. Its diagnostic value for separating borderline from benign tumors is low; it should not guide decisions for that distinction, particularly decisions about fertility-sparing procedures.

document_sections.heading: Statements on MRI, CT, and PET/CT (Statements 13–17)
document_sections.content: Statement 13: MRI incorporating dynamic contrast-enhanced and diffusion-weighted functional sequences is not first-line imaging, but may be used after ultrasound to further distinguish benign, malignant and borderline masses. Level of evidence: 2a; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 100% (n=20), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 0% (n=0). Statement 14: If initial ultrasound suggests secondary metastasis, PET-CT and whole-body diffusion MRI can be useful second-step examinations for detecting a non-ovarian primary site. Level of evidence: 4; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 90% (n=18), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 10% (n=2). Statement 15: PET-CT does not reliably distinguish borderline from benign tumors. Level of evidence: 4; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 95% (n=19), no, 0% (n=0), abstain, 5% (n=1). Statement 16: Imaging by itself cannot reliably show the full extent of peritoneal carcinomatosis, particularly low-volume disease, or mesenteric and bowel serosal involvement. Level of evidence: 3b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 85% (n=17), no, 5% (n=1), abstain, 10% (n=2). Statement 17: Prediction of peritoneal tumor resectability and related surgical decisions should not rely on imaging alone. Level of evidence: 3b; Grade of statement: B; consensus yes, 80% (n=16), no, 15% (n=3), abstain, 5% (n=1).

document_sections.heading: Circulating cell-free DNA and circulating tumor cells
document_sections.content: Studies have investigated circulating cell-free DNA and circulating tumor cells as non-invasive cancer markers and components of liquid biopsy. Methylation patterns in cell-free DNA might identify some ovarian cancers up to 2 years before diagnosis and could potentially guide personalized treatment, but validation is lacking. Collection vials that stabilize blood cells and limit background DNA contamination may facilitate clinical use. A prospective evaluation using chromosomal instability suggested cell-free DNA could improve the specificity of pre-surgical malignancy prediction in patients with adnexal masses. These circulating markers inform research into metastasis, tumor formation and changes during treatment and progression, but are not established in routine practice. One meta-analysis found quantitative cell-free DNA analysis insufficiently sensitive but acceptably specific for ovarian cancer diagnosis. A more recent meta-analysis suggested diagnostic discrimination slightly better than CA 125 and similar to HE4. Its diagnostic value in ovarian cancer remains uncertain, so those results require caution. Large prospective studies are strongly recommended to validate cell-free DNA alone or with conventional markers and investigate factors affecting diagnostic accuracy.

document_sections.heading: Statement on circulating cell-free DNA and tumor cells (Statement 18)
document_sections.content: Statement 18: Circulating cell-free DNA and circulating tumor cells should not yet be used routinely to distinguish benign from malignant ovarian masses. Level of evidence: 4; Grade of statement: C; consensus yes, 85% (n=17), no, 5% (n=1), abstain, 10% (n=2).

document_sections.heading: OVERVIEW OF CONSENSUS
document_sections.content: The experts agreed on a flowchart for distinguishing benign from malignant tumors and selecting care pathways. Ultrasound is recommended first for symptoms suggesting an adnexal mass or an incidental mass on imaging. Once normal ovaries and physiological changes have been ruled out—that is, O-RADS 1 has been excluded—IOTA ADNEX could be used to estimate malignancy risk. Suspected ovarian masses should undergo ultrasound assessment by an expert sonographer. Classification into O-RADS categories 2–5 can inform management and referral to a dedicated gynecological oncology center. A further agreed pathway addresses malignant subtypes and disease extent within those centers. Expert ultrasound assessment or IOTA ADNEX combined with CA 125 and CEA, with other markers in selected cases, can often suggest the subtype. Where available, diffusion- and perfusion-weighted MRI can confirm characterization of the primary lesion, especially when fertility-sparing surgery is contemplated. Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is mandatory to exclude secondary cancers, thromboembolic events and multifocal intraparenchymal distant metastases that preclude resectability. An expert multidisciplinary team should determine the final individualized pathway using diagnostic results together with symptoms, preferences, and prior surgical, medical and reproductive history.

conditions.name: adnexal masses
conditions.description: Adnexal masses require characterization before treatment decisions so that benign lesions, ovarian malignancies and tumors originating outside the gynecological tract can be distinguished.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A mass may be suspected because of symptoms or discovered incidentally on imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the mass and distinguish benign from malignant disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: First imaging assessment of suspected or incidentally detected adnexal pathology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diagnostic accuracy depends on examiner expertise; expert subjective assessment performs particularly well.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify characteristic benign or malignant appearances.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of an adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The descriptors can classify about 43% of adnexal masses immediately.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify a mass using benign and malignant ultrasound features.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of an adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The rules apply to about 80% of masses; other results are inconclusive.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate an individual probability of malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of an adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A multicenter comparison identified this and the IOTA ADNEX model as the best-performing models among those compared for mass characterization.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate malignancy risk and distinguish categories of malignant disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After ultrasound has excluded normal ovaries and physiological changes, or during specialist characterization of a mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The model distinguishes benign tumors, borderline tumors, Stage I and Stage II–IV primary cancers, and secondary metastatic tumors. A predicted secondary metastatic tumor risk above 10% triggers further investigation of the primary site.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify adnexal masses using CA 125, menopausal status and ultrasound findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Pre-operative assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It does not yield an estimated malignancy risk and depends substantially on CA 125; sensitivity is relatively low for early-stage invasive and borderline disease, particularly before menopause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess ovarian malignancy using CA 125 and HE4.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Pre-operative assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neither ROMA nor HE4 improves benign-versus-malignant discrimination over CA 125 alone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assign an ultrasound-based category of malignancy probability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of an adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The categories span GI-RADS 1 through GI-RADS 5.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Describe ultrasound appearances and stratify adnexal masses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Ultrasound assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The ultrasound descriptors and triage system had not been externally validated at the time of the statement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further distinguish benign, borderline and malignant masses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Second-line assessment after ultrasound, particularly when ultrasound remains indeterminate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Functional sequences include dynamic contrast-enhanced and diffusion-weighted MRI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help characterize a suspicious mass and differentiate malignant subtypes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It is not useful for ovarian cancer screening and does not improve ultrasound-based risk models for benign-versus-malignant discrimination. Age, pregnancy, inflammatory processes, fibroids, endometriosis, body mass index and ethnicity can affect its level.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish primary ovarian malignancy from a secondary ovarian tumor.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases in which metastatic disease is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help identify secondary metastatic tumors in the ovary.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases.

staging.additional_rules: The document notes that the boundary between early and advanced disease differs between ADNEX model categories and oncological stage groupings; it does not provide full stage definitions.

prognostic_tools.name: IOTA Simple Descriptors
components: BD1: a pre-menopausal woman's unilocular mass with ground-glass echogenicity
BD2: a pre-menopausal woman's unilocular mass with mixed echogenicity and acoustic shadows
BD3: an anechoic unilocular mass with regular walls and maximum diameter <10 cm
BD4: another unilocular mass with regular walls
MD1: ascites and at least moderate color Doppler flow in a post-menopausal woman
MD2: age >50 years and CA 125 >100 U/mL
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Provides a descriptor-based classification rather than a numerical risk estimate.

prognostic_tools.name: RMI
components: Ultrasound score incorporating multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites and abdominal-ultrasound evidence of metastases
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Produces a score but not an individual estimated probability of malignancy.

prognostic_tools.name: ROMA
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Does not improve benign-versus-malignant discrimination compared with CA 125 alone.

prognostic_tools.name: IOTA Simple Rules
components: Benign features: unilocular cyst; smooth multilocular cyst with largest diameter <100 mm; solid areas with largest diameter <7 mm; acoustic shadows; absence of color Doppler vascularization
Malignant features: irregular solid tumor; irregular multilocular solid tumor with largest diameter ≥100 mm; ascites; ≥4 papillary projections; very strong color Doppler vascularization

risk_groups.criteria: Classification according to the benign and malignant ultrasound features.
The ultrasound features do not permit a benign or malignant classification.
Classification according to the benign and malignant ultrasound features.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Classifies masses without providing a numerical risk estimate.

prognostic_tools.name: LR1
prognostic_tools.interpretation: An IOTA logistic regression model that outperformed the comparator models, including RMI, in the cited external validation study.

prognostic_tools.name: LR2
components: Maximum diameter of the largest solid component

prognostic_tools.name: IOTA Simple Rules risk model
components: The 10 binary features of IOTA Simple Rules
Type of center: oncology center or other
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Adds an individual risk estimate to the Simple Rules features.

prognostic_tools.name: IOTA ADNEX model
components: Maximum diameter of the largest solid component (mm)
Type of center: oncology center or other
Serum CA 125 (IU/L) in the version with CA 125

risk_groups.criteria: Model-estimated tumor category; a predicted risk above 10% triggers investigation of the primary organ.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Estimates both overall malignancy risk and risks for malignant subtypes; versions with and without CA 125 are described.

prognostic_tools.name: GI-RADS
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Groups adnexal masses by estimated probability of malignancy.

prognostic_tools.name: O-RADS
components: Alternatively, malignancy risk assigned by the IOTA ADNEX model
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Provides ultrasound-based risk categories; its descriptors and triage system had not undergone external validation at the time of the statement.

conditions.name: Endometrioma
conditions.description: An endometriosis-related adnexal tumor that is typically uni- or multilocular.
conditions.epidemiology: The table reports a median age of 34.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize the characteristic lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually has 1–4 locules with ground-glass contents. Papillations occur in 10%, most often without internal blood flow.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: An elevated value can accompany this endometriosis-related lesion.

conditions.name: Fibroma/fibrothecoma
conditions.description: A predominantly solid sex cord-stromal tumor with a generally regular outline.
conditions.epidemiology: The table gives a median age of 50 and reports that 65% are postmenopausal.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the solid adnexal tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically round, oval or mildly lobulated, with fan-shaped shadowing; 15–20% are multilocular-solid.

conditions.name: Sertoli cell tumor
conditions.description: A sex cord-stromal tumor described as mostly benign.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The tumor may be hormonally inactive or produce estrogen, in which case abnormal bleeding can occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the adnexal tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral and solid, with median diameter 90 mm.

conditions.name: Leydig cell tumor
conditions.description: A solid sex cord-stromal tumor described as almost always benign.
conditions.epidemiology: The table gives a median age of 58.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Endocrine symptoms occur, with virilization reported in 75%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the adnexal tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral and solid, with median diameter 24 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the endocrine presentation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected hormonally active tumor.

conditions.name: Mature cystic teratoma
conditions.description: A germ cell tumor with a characteristic heterogeneous cystic appearance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the characteristic appearance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A unilocular appearance occurs in 58%; multilocular or solid-containing patterns also occur. Mixed echogenicity, a white ball, stripes and shadowing are typical.

conditions.name: Struma ovarii
conditions.description: An ovarian teratoma made entirely or predominantly of thyroid tissue; it represents 3% of all ovarian teratomas.
conditions.epidemiology: The table reports a median age of 40.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize the characteristic morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually multilocular or multilocular-solid, with anechoic or low-level fluid; a smooth, rounded solid area may form a struma pearl. Papillations are uncommon.

conditions.name: Serous cystadenoma
conditions.description: A benign epithelial adnexal tumor with a usually uni- or multilocular cystic appearance.
conditions.epidemiology: The table lists age 40–60 and unilateral occurrence in 80–90%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize cystic morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically has 2–10 locules when multilocular, anechoic fluid and often papillations lacking internal blood flow.

conditions.name: Serous cystadenofibroma
conditions.description: A benign epithelial tumor that may contain cystic and solid components.
conditions.epidemiology: The table lists age 40–60 and unilateral occurrence in 84%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize the tumor's characteristic morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Patterns are multilocular-solid (37%), unilocular-solid (30%), multilocular (19%) or unilocular (13%); median diameter is 50–80 mm. Papillations number 1 (52%), 2 (17%) or 3 (13%); absent color Doppler signals occur in 80% and shadowing behind papillations in 40%.

conditions.name: Mucinous cystadenoma
conditions.description: A benign epithelial tumor, most commonly multilocular.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize tumor morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multilocular morphology occurs in 65%, often with >10 locules; unilocular morphology occurs in 18% and multilocular-solid morphology in 16%. Median diameter is 112 mm, and a honeycomb nodule may be seen.

conditions.name: Brenner tumor
conditions.description: An epithelial tumor described as benign in 99%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify characteristic tumor features.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually a small unilateral solid tumor measuring 20–80 mm, frequently with extensive calcification, small internal cysts and shadowing; it can also be multilocular-solid.

conditions.name: Abscess
conditions.description: An infection-related adnexal lesion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can be unilateral or bilateral and uni- or multilocular, with a cogwheel appearance and mixed echogenicity.

conditions.name: Borderline serous
conditions.description: A borderline epithelial adnexal tumor frequently showing vascularized papillary projections.
conditions.epidemiology: Median age is 42; 30% are <40. Tumors are unilateral in 73% and bilateral in 27%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a characteristic borderline tumor appearance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Unilocular-solid morphology occurs in 55% and multilocular-solid morphology in 30%; fluid is anechoic in 47% or has low-level echoes. More than 3 irregular papillations occur in 81%, with internal flow and anechoic spaces but without shadowing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further distinguish a borderline mass from benign or malignant alternatives.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Second-line assessment after ultrasound when further characterization is needed.

conditions.name: Borderline mucinous (intestinal type)
conditions.description: A borderline epithelial tumor that is often large and contains numerous small cystic compartments.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize a suspected borderline tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually unilateral; multilocular morphology occurs in 80% and unilocular morphology in 15%. Median diameter is 195 mm. Small locules and a honeycomb nodule are common; papillations are absent and fluid has low-level echoes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further distinguish borderline disease from benign or malignant masses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Second-line assessment after ultrasound when needed.

conditions.name: Borderline mucinous (endocervical type)
conditions.description: A borderline epithelial tumor with a usually unilocular-solid appearance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize tumor morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually unilateral and unilocular-solid, sometimes multilocular-solid, with median diameter 37 mm. Papillations occur in 60%; fluid can have low-level or ground-glass echoes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further characterize a borderline mass.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Second-line assessment after ultrasound when needed.

conditions.name: Borderline seromucinous
conditions.description: A borderline tumor containing endometrioid-, indifferent- and squamous-type epithelium.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The table describes unilateral occurrence but does not specify a characteristic ultrasound pattern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further distinguish borderline disease from other masses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Second-line assessment after ultrasound when needed.

conditions.name: Low-grade serous carcinoma
conditions.description: An epithelial ovarian carcinoma that often has both cystic and solid components.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multilocular-solid morphology occurs in 55% and solid morphology in 32%. Small calcifications may occur in solid tissue; papillations occur in 32%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and exclude findings that would preclude resectability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is required; imaging alone cannot reliably establish complete peritoneal tumor resectability.

conditions.name: High-grade serous carcinoma
conditions.description: An epithelial ovarian carcinoma commonly appearing predominantly solid.
conditions.epidemiology: The table lists age 55–65 and bilateral occurrence in 50%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Solid morphology occurs in 64% and multilocular-solid morphology in 33%. Solid tissue can contain necrosis; papillations occur in 7%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and exclude findings that would preclude resectability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Chest, abdominal and pelvic imaging is required, but imaging alone does not reliably predict peritoneal tumor resectability.

conditions.name: Mucinous carcinoma
conditions.description: An epithelial ovarian carcinoma often forming a very large mass.
conditions.epidemiology: The table identifies this subtype as 3% of malignant tumors, gives a median age of 53 and reports unilateral occurrence in 80%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multilocular-solid morphology occurs in 55%; the mass can also be multilocular or solid. Median diameter is 197 mm, and cystic fluid has low-level echoes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and exclude secondary cancers and findings that would preclude resectability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional imaging when clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected diagnostic questions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Lower fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in invasive mucinous tumors can impair diagnostic performance.

conditions.name: Endometrioid carcinoma
conditions.description: An epithelial ovarian carcinoma that can arise from endometriosis.
conditions.epidemiology: The table identifies this subtype as 10–15%, gives a median age of 55 and reports unilateral occurrence in 79%. Coexisting endometrial carcinoma occurs in 20%; 20% develop from endometriosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multilocular-solid morphology occurs in 48%, with low-level fluid in 53% or ground-glass fluid in 16%; solid morphology occurs in 34%. Median diameter is 102 mm. A cockade-like appearance may occur, and papillations are present in 29%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and findings relevant to surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.

conditions.name: Clear cell carcinoma
conditions.description: An epithelial ovarian carcinoma that can develop from endometriosis.
conditions.epidemiology: The table identifies this subtype as 5–25%, gives a median age of 55 and reports unilateral occurrence in 85%. Development from endometriosis is reported in 20–30%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Multilocular-solid morphology occurs in 41% and unilocular-solid morphology in 35%, with low-level fluid in 44% or ground-glass fluid in 22%; solid morphology occurs in 24%. Median diameter is 117 mm; solid nodules occur, and papillations are seen in 38%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and findings relevant to surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional imaging when clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected diagnostic questions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Lower fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in invasive clear cell tumors can impair diagnostic performance.

conditions.name: Carcinosarcoma
conditions.description: An ovarian malignancy usually forming a solid mass with irregular margins and cystic areas.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the ovarian malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Solid morphology occurs in 72.5% and multilocular-solid morphology in 24.5%; median diameter is 100 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extent and findings relevant to surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before planned surgery for presumed malignancy.

conditions.name: Granulosa cell tumor
conditions.description: A sex cord-stromal tumor that can show hemorrhage and necrosis within heterogeneous solid tissue.
conditions.epidemiology: The table reports 70% for this tumor category; 50% are premenopausal and 3–10% are prepubertal in the juvenile type.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Hyper-estrogenic manifestations can include abnormal bleeding and a thickened endometrium.

subtypes.name: juvenile type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The table associates this type with prepubertal presentation in 3–10%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the sex cord-stromal tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually a large unilateral multilocular-solid or solid mass, with median diameter 100 mm, heterogeneous solid tissue, mixed or low-level fluid echoes and occasionally papillations. A Swiss cheese pattern is described.

conditions.name: Sertoli-Leydig-cell tumor
conditions.description: A sex cord-stromal tumor that can appear solid or multilocular-solid.
conditions.epidemiology: Age is ≤30 in 75%; the table reports unilateral occurrence in 100%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Endocrine symptoms occur; one-third have virilization.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually a large multilocular-solid or solid mass with median diameter 50–150 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess endocrine manifestations.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected hormonally active tumor.

conditions.name: Dysgerminoma
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy with a highly vascular, lobulated solid appearance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize characteristic tumor morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral and entirely solid, with heterogeneous internal echogenicity arranged in lobules and a smooth or lobulated contour well demarcated from nearby organs.

conditions.name: Yolk sac tumor
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy that commonly forms a large irregular mass.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually unilateral, multilocular-solid or solid and 100–200 mm in size, with finely textured, slightly hyperechoic solid tissue.

conditions.name: Immature teratoma
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy with a predominantly solid, highly heterogeneous appearance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually a large unilateral mass with markedly heterogeneous solid tissue and hyper-reflective areas.

conditions.name: Choriocarcinoma
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy appearing as a large solid mass with small irregular cystic spaces.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral, large and solid, with heterogeneous echogenicity and small irregular cystic spaces.

conditions.name: Embryonal carcinoma
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy appearing as a large heterogeneous solid mass with small irregular cystic spaces.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral and large, with heterogeneous solid tissue and small irregular cystic spaces.

conditions.name: Malignant mixed germ cell tumor
conditions.description: A germ cell malignancy appearing as a large heterogeneous solid mass with small irregular cystic spaces.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the tumor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typically unilateral and large, with heterogeneous solid tissue and small irregular cystic spaces.

conditions.name: secondary metastatic tumors
conditions.description: Tumors in the ovary originating from a non-ovarian primary site; the document distinguishes characteristic patterns associated with different primary organs.

subtypes.name: Breast, stomach, lymphoma or uterus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The table describes a usually solid ovarian mass with median diameter 70 mm and a lead-vessel sign; bilateral occurrence is reported in 50–75%.

subtypes.name: Colon, rectum, appendix or biliary tract
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The table describes a multilocular or multilocular-solid, irregular mass with many locules and papillations, median diameter 120 mm; bilateral occurrence is reported in 50–75%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify features suggesting a metastatic rather than primary ovarian tumor.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of an ovarian mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The described appearances vary with the organ of origin.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the probability that an ovarian tumor is secondary metastatic disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Characterization of an adnexal mass.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A predicted risk above 10% triggers additional investigation to find the primary organ.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to differentiation of malignant tumor subtypes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The table reports moderate elevation in 75% for both listed groups of metastatic primaries.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish secondary ovarian disease from primary ovarian cancer.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases, particularly when a gastrointestinal primary is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The table associates elevation with colon or rectum primaries.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish metastatic disease in the ovary.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases.
